subject: computing
title: KS3 Computing — Legal & Ethical Issues in Computing
subtitle: UK computing laws, ethical dilemmas, AI bias, surveillance, and digital rights.

data.targetWord: UK law from 1990 that makes it a criminal offence to access computer systems or data without authorisation, or to modify computer material without permission

examples.en-GB: Under the Computer Misuse Act, guessing a classmate's password and logging into their account is a criminal offence.

data.targetWord: UK law (updated 2018, based on UK GDPR) that governs how organisations must collect, store, use, and protect individuals' personal data

examples.en-GB: Under the Data Protection Act, a company must have a valid reason to collect personal data and can only use it for the purpose stated.

data.targetWord: General Data Protection Regulation — the EU data protection framework adopted into UK law, giving individuals rights over their personal data and placing obligations on organisations that process it

examples.en-GB: GDPR gives individuals the right to access all personal data held about them and the right to request its deletion.

data.targetWord: the legal protection automatically granted to the creator of an original work, giving them exclusive rights to copy, distribute, or modify it

examples.en-GB: Copyright automatically protects software code, meaning you cannot legally copy and distribute someone else's program without permission.

data.targetWord: creative works or inventions that belong to their creator and are protected by law through copyright, patents, or trademarks

examples.en-GB: Software code is intellectual property; using it without a licence can result in legal action under copyright law.

data.targetWord: software whose source code is publicly available and freely accessible, typically under a licence that specifies how it may be used, modified, and distributed

examples.en-GB: Linux is open source software; anyone can view the code, contribute improvements, and distribute modified versions under its licence terms.

data.targetWord: a set of standardised licences that allow creators to specify exactly what others may do with their work, such as allowing free use with attribution

examples.en-GB: A Creative Commons licence can allow teachers to use and share an image freely as long as they credit the original creator.

data.targetWord: UK law from 2000 that requires public sector organisations to disclose information about their activities upon request, within 20 working days

examples.en-GB: A citizen used the Freedom of Information Act to request details of how the council's CCTV data is stored and processed.

data.targetWord: gaining unauthorised access to a computer system or network, typically to steal data, plant malware, or cause disruption

examples.en-GB: Hacking into a company's database to steal customer details is an offence under the Computer Misuse Act.

data.targetWord: accessing a computer system, network, or data without the permission of the owner or administrator — the first offence under the Computer Misuse Act

examples.en-GB: Reading a colleague's private emails by guessing their password counts as unauthorised access under the Computer Misuse Act.

data.targetWord: an incident in which personal or sensitive data is accessed, disclosed, or lost without authorisation, which must be reported to the ICO within 72 hours

examples.en-GB: The organisation reported the data breach to the ICO within 72 hours as required by the Data Protection Act.

data.targetWord: any information that can identify a living individual, including names, email addresses, location data, and IP addresses, which is protected under the Data Protection Act

examples.en-GB: Under the Data Protection Act, personal data such as a customer's name, address, and purchase history must be stored securely.

data.targetWord: explicit, informed agreement from an individual to allow an organisation to collect and use their personal data for a stated purpose

examples.en-GB: Organisations must obtain clear consent before collecting personal data; burying it in lengthy terms and conditions may not count as genuine consent.

data.targetWord: a moral question about whether an action is right or wrong, regardless of its legality — something that may be legal but that many people consider unfair or harmful

examples.en-GB: Selling user data with buried consent in terms and conditions may be legal but is still considered an ethical issue by many.

data.targetWord: something that is prohibited by law, where breaking the rule can result in prosecution, fines, or imprisonment

examples.en-GB: Accessing someone else's computer without permission is a legal issue — it is a criminal offence under the Computer Misuse Act.

data.targetWord: discrimination embedded in an artificial intelligence system because the data it was trained on reflected historical biases or inequalities

examples.en-GB: An AI recruitment tool showed AI bias by favouring male candidates because the training data reflected a historically male-dominated workforce.

data.targetWord: the monitoring of individuals' movements, activities, or communications, typically by governments or organisations using CCTV, facial recognition, or data collection

examples.en-GB: The use of facial recognition cameras in public spaces raises ethical concerns about surveillance and invasion of privacy.

data.targetWord: the use of technology — robots, AI, or software — to perform tasks that were previously done by humans

examples.en-GB: Automation in manufacturing has increased efficiency but has also displaced workers whose jobs have been replaced by robots.

data.targetWord: the gap between those who have access to technology and digital skills and those who do not, creating inequality in education, employment, and access to services

examples.en-GB: The digital divide became visible during the pandemic when students without home computers could not access remote learning.

data.targetWord: the principle that someone must be held responsible when an AI or algorithmic system causes harm, and that its decisions must be explainable and auditable

examples.en-GB: Algorithmic accountability is a major concern when AI systems make important decisions about loan applications or medical diagnoses.

data.targetWord: an individual's right to control what information about them is collected, stored, and shared by others

examples.en-GB: Collecting location data from a user's phone without their knowledge is a violation of their privacy.

data.targetWord: criminal activity carried out using computers or the internet, including hacking, fraud, ransomware attacks, and identity theft

examples.en-GB: Ransomware attacks are a form of cybercrime in which criminals encrypt victims' files and demand payment for the key.

data.targetWord: laws that have been passed by a parliament or government body; computing legislation includes acts such as the Computer Misuse Act and Data Protection Act

examples.en-GB: UK computing legislation covers a wide range of activities, from unauthorised access to data protection and copyright infringement.

data.targetWord: Information Commissioner's Office — the UK regulator that enforces the Data Protection Act and can issue fines of up to £17.5 million for serious breaches

examples.en-GB: The ICO fined the company for failing to protect customer data and not reporting the breach within 72 hours.

data.targetWord: legal permission granted by a creator or rights holder that specifies how software or other copyrighted material may be used, distributed, or modified

examples.en-GB: The software came with a licence allowing it to be installed on one computer only; copying it to additional machines would be illegal.

data.targetWord: the principle that some actions or disclosures are justified because they benefit society as a whole, even if they might otherwise be restricted

examples.en-GB: Disclosing information about unsafe government practices may be justified in the public interest under the Freedom of Information Act.

data.targetWord: the act of reporting illegal or unethical activities within an organisation to authorities or the public, often by an employee

examples.en-GB: A whistleblower revealed that the tech company was unlawfully sharing user data, leading to a major ICO investigation.

data.targetWord: treating individuals unfairly based on characteristics such as gender, race, age, or disability, which may occur when biased AI systems make decisions about people

examples.en-GB: An AI trained on biased historical data may result in algorithmic discrimination, disproportionately rejecting loan applications from certain groups.

data.targetWord: a formal request made by an individual under the Data Protection Act to receive a copy of all personal data that an organisation holds about them

examples.en-GB: She submitted a Subject Access Request to the hospital to find out what medical data they held about her.

data.targetWord: rules made by a regulatory body that organisations must follow, often to ensure they comply with legislation such as the Data Protection Act

examples.en-GB: The ICO's regulation of data protection ensures that organisations handle personal data responsibly and lawfully.

data.sentence: The Computer Misuse Act ____ makes unauthorised access to computer systems a criminal offence.
The Data Protection Act 2018 is based on the UK ____ framework, which gives individuals rights over their personal data.
The Copyright, Designs and Patents Act ____ protects creators' original works from being copied without permission.
Individuals have the right to access their own personal data by submitting a ____ Access Request to an organisation.
Organisations must report significant data breaches to the ICO within ____ hours.
AI ____ occurs when a system is trained on biased historical data and perpetuates those biases in its decisions.
A ____ issue is something prohibited by law; an ethical issue is something morally questionable even if it is legal.
Removing names from a dataset does not always make it ____ because individuals can sometimes be re-identified from other data.
Copyright covers software, images, music, text, and databases — not just ____ and films.
The ____ of Information Act 2000 requires public sector organisations to disclose information about their activities on request.
The ICO (Information Commissioner's Office) enforces the Data Protection Act and can issue fines of up to £____ million.
Under the Data Protection Act, personal data must only be used for the specific ____ for which it was originally collected.
Offence 3 of the Computer Misuse Act criminalises unauthorised ____ of computer material, such as planting a virus or deleting files.
____ source software has publicly available code and a licence specifying how it may be used or modified.
____ licences allow creators to specify permitted uses of their work, such as 'free to use with attribution'.
When AI causes harm and nobody knows who is responsible, this raises concerns about algorithmic ____.
____ is both a legal offence under the Computer Misuse Act and widely considered an ethical issue.
The digital ____ describes the gap between those with and without access to technology and digital skills.
The Data Protection Act states that data must be stored securely and only for as long as ____ for its purpose.
Offence 1 of the Computer Misuse Act covers unauthorised ____ to a computer system, even if no damage is caused.
A ____ is someone who exposes illegal or unethical practices within an organisation, often at personal risk.
Arguments for ____ include increased efficiency and removing humans from dangerous jobs, but it can also cause job displacement.

data.title: What must happen when a company suffers a data breach?
data.instruction: Arrange these steps in the correct order to describe the required response to a data breach under the Data Protection Act.
items: Detect and identify the data breach
Assess the scope and risk to individuals
Report the breach to the ICO within 72 hours
Notify the affected individuals if there is high risk to them
Document the breach and the actions taken

data.title: Three offences of the Computer Misuse Act in order of severity
data.instruction: Arrange the three offences of the Computer Misuse Act from least severe to most severe.
items: Offence 1: Unauthorised access to computer material
Offence 2: Unauthorised access with intent to commit a further offence
Offence 3: Unauthorised modification of computer material

data.title: Legal issue, ethical issue, or both?
data.instruction: Sort each computing scenario into the correct category.

pairs.text: Hacking into a company's database to steal credit card numbers
Selling user data to advertisers without genuine informed consent
Developing an AI that has been trained on biased data
Copying and distributing software without a licence
Collecting more personal data than necessary for a stated purpose
Designing an app that is difficult for elderly users to use
Accessing a colleague's files without their permission
Deploying facial recognition that has higher error rates for people of colour

data.title: Which UK law applies to this scenario?
data.instruction: Sort each scenario into the law that applies to it.

pairs.text: Guessing a classmate's password and reading their emails
Deploying ransomware that encrypts a hospital's files
A company selling customer email addresses without consent
A business failing to report a data breach to the ICO
Downloading and distributing a film without paying for it
Using someone else's code in your project without a licence

data.title: Arguments for or against AI surveillance?
data.instruction: Sort each argument into whether it supports or opposes the use of AI surveillance in public spaces.

pairs.text: It can deter crime and make public spaces safer
It helps identify suspects after crimes have been committed
It can help locate missing persons quickly
It is a serious invasion of privacy for innocent people
Facial recognition has higher error rates for people of colour
It has a chilling effect on freedom of expression and assembly
Collected data can be misused by governments or companies
